title: Complete Data Analysis with Excel, Power BI & Google Sheets Certificate
description: A full 20-module program from complete beginner to job-ready data analyst: data fundamentals, Excel (essentials, formulas, advanced), Google Sheets, data cleaning, visualization, Power BI (fundamentals & advanced), business intelligence & reporting, statistics, AI for data, data storytelling, SQL, 10 real-world dashboards, a capstone and a Certificate of Completion.
outcomes: Collect, clean, analyse, visualise and present data
Master Microsoft Excel: formulas, functions, pivot tables and dashboards
Use Google Sheets (incl. QUERY, FILTER, ARRAYFORMULA) and Power BI
Build interactive dashboards and business intelligence reports
Apply statistics, write basic SQL, and use AI to speed up analysis
Tell data stories and build a job-ready analytics portfolio
about: This is the complete TIH Data Analysis Certificate, rebuilt into twenty modules that take you from complete beginner to job-ready data analyst across Excel, Power BI and Google Sheets.

Every content lesson has a video and printable notes with downloadable practice files; ten real-world dashboards and a capstone build a portfolio for roles like Data Analyst, Business Analyst and M&E Officer.

Software & tools: Microsoft Excel, Power BI Desktop & Service, Google Sheets & Forms, Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, SQL (MySQL/PostgreSQL), PowerPoint, Google Slides, GitHub and Kaggle datasets. You finish with a portfolio and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion.
requirements: No prior experience required — we start from the basics
A computer with Excel (or Google Sheets) and internet access
Willingness to practise on real datasets

faqs.question: Do I need to buy Microsoft Excel?
faqs.answer: You can use the free Google Sheets for most modules. Microsoft Excel 2016+ is recommended but the free 30-day Microsoft trial is sufficient to complete the course.

faqs.question: How is this different from the Office course?
faqs.answer: The Office course covers Excel basics for general use. This Data course goes much deeper into analytics, advanced functions, pivot tables, and Power BI for professional data work.

faqs.question: Will I be able to get a data analyst job after this?
faqs.answer: This course builds strong foundational data skills. Combined with practice projects, many graduates have secured data analyst, reporting, and business intelligence roles.

faqs.question: Are the datasets used in lessons realistic?
faqs.answer: Yes. All practice datasets are modeled on real Liberian and West African business scenarios, NGO reports, retail sales, health data, and government statistics.

instructor.name: Emmanuel Kamara
instructor.title: Senior Data Analyst & Business Intelligence Trainer
instructor.bio: Emmanuel Kamara has over 8 years of experience in business intelligence and data analytics, having worked with NGOs, government agencies, and private firms across West Africa. He specializes in making data analysis accessible to non-technical professionals.

lessons.title: 1.1 Welcome to the Course
lessons.html:
Data Analysis · Module 1Excel · Power BI · Google Sheets

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Welcome to the Course

Welcome to the Course is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It develops the learner’s ability to apply this analytical method correctly, verify the result, and explain what it means.

Data analysis

The systematic process of collecting, cleaning, exploring, interpreting, and communicating data.

dataset

An organised collection of related observations or records.

insight

A useful conclusion supported by analysed evidence.

🧭 Welcome to the Course
Understand the method, work through the data, verify the result, and explain the decision it supports.

Welcome to the Course

Definition

Welcome to the Course is a practical part of Course Orientation: the complete process used to turn raw data into evidence for decisions. The skill is complete only when the result is correct, reproducible, and understandable to its intended audience.

Detailed explanation

A clear analytical process prevents tools and charts from replacing the real business question. For this topic, begin with the business or research question, identify the required fields and units, then choose the simplest method that answers the question accurately.

Do not accept a result because the software produced it. Check source quality, formulas, filters, relationships, and comparison periods. The analyst—not the tool—remains responsible for the meaning of the result.

Step-by-step analytical workflow

  1. Define the analytical question, audience, period, units, and success measure.
  2. Inspect and clean the source before calculating or visualising anything.
  3. Apply Welcome to the Course with the appropriate spreadsheet, Power BI, or SQL method.
  4. Cross-check totals, filters, data types, missing values, and assumptions.
  5. Explain the finding, limitation, and recommended decision in plain language.

Worked data example

RegionTargetActualVariance
Montserrado100118+18
Bong9081−9
Nimba110126+16

Method or formula:

Question → Data → Analysis → Decision

Interpretation: In this sample, Montserrado and Nimba exceeded their targets while Bong was below target. A useful analyst would investigate why, check whether the comparison periods and units are consistent, and then recommend a specific action rather than reporting the numbers alone.

A
B
C
D

How to read this chart: Compare the bar heights to find the largest and smallest categories. A line chart would be more suitable if A–D represented consecutive time periods and the main question concerned change over time.

Professional best practices

  • Define the question before opening a tool.
  • Record assumptions, sources, and limitations.
  • Explain the result in language the audience can act on.

Common mistakes and professional corrections

Common mistakeCorrection
Starting with a chart before defining the questionWrite the decision question and audience first.
Using unclean or inconsistently formatted dataProfile, clean, document, and validate the source.
Reporting a number without contextCompare it with a target, prior period, benchmark, or relevant segment.
📊 Practical task: Apply Welcome to the Course to a small dataset from a school, shop, NGO, clinic, or public source. Save the working file, show the calculation or transformation, create one appropriate visual, and write a two-sentence insight and recommendation.

Chart-selection guide

  • Comparison: use a bar or column chart.
  • Trend over time: use a line chart.
  • Distribution: use a histogram or box plot.
  • Relationship: use a scatter plot.
  • Composition: use a stacked bar; use a pie only for a few simple parts of one whole.

Summary

Welcome to the Course belongs to Course Orientation. A capable analyst can explain the method, apply it to clean data, audit the result, select a truthful visual, and communicate the insight and recommended action.

Study tip: Keep the raw source unchanged. Work in a copy, label every transformation, and independently check one total before trusting the dashboard.

Data Entry Techniques

Definition

Data Entry Techniques is a practical part of Microsoft Excel Essentials: using Microsoft Excel workbooks, worksheets, cells, tables, formatting, and controls to manage data. The skill is complete only when the result is correct, reproducible, and understandable to its intended audience.

Detailed explanation

Excel is widely used in business, government, banking, education, and NGOs because it combines data entry, calculation, and reporting. For this topic, begin with the business or research question, identify the required fields and units, then choose the simplest method that answers the question accurately.

Do not accept a result because the software produced it. Check source quality, formulas, filters, relationships, and comparison periods. The analyst—not the tool—remains responsible for the meaning of the result.

Step-by-step analytical workflow

  1. Define the analytical question, audience, period, units, and success measure.
  2. Inspect and clean the source before calculating or visualising anything.
  3. Apply Data Entry Techniques with the appropriate spreadsheet, Power BI, or SQL method.
  4. Cross-check totals, filters, data types, missing values, and assumptions.
  5. Explain the finding, limitation, and recommended decision in plain language.

Worked data example

RegionTargetActualVariance
Montserrado100118+18
Bong9081−9
Nimba110126+16

Method or formula:

Ctrl+T → My table has headers → Apply

Interpretation: In this sample, Montserrado and Nimba exceeded their targets while Bong was below target. A useful analyst would investigate why, check whether the comparison periods and units are consistent, and then recommend a specific action rather than reporting the numbers alone.

A
B
C
D

How to read this chart: Compare the bar heights to find the largest and smallest categories. A line chart would be more suitable if A–D represented consecutive time periods and the main question concerned change over time.

Professional best practices

  • Keep one variable in each column.
  • Use tables instead of unstructured coloured ranges.
  • Never mix totals or titles inside the raw-data table.

Common mistakes and professional corrections

Common mistakeCorrection
Starting with a chart before defining the questionWrite the decision question and audience first.
Using unclean or inconsistently formatted dataProfile, clean, document, and validate the source.
Reporting a number without contextCompare it with a target, prior period, benchmark, or relevant segment.
📊 Practical task: Apply Data Entry Techniques to a small dataset from a school, shop, NGO, clinic, or public source. Save the working file, show the calculation or transformation, create one appropriate visual, and write a two-sentence insight and recommendation.

Chart-selection guide

  • Comparison: use a bar or column chart.
  • Trend over time: use a line chart.
  • Distribution: use a histogram or box plot.
  • Relationship: use a scatter plot.
  • Composition: use a stacked bar; use a pie only for a few simple parts of one whole.

Summary

Data Entry Techniques belongs to Microsoft Excel Essentials. A capable analyst can explain the method, apply it to clean data, audit the result, select a truthful visual, and communicate the insight and recommended action.

lessons.html:
Data Analysis · Module 4Excel · Power BI · Google Sheets

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Practice Exercises

Practice Exercises is the focus of this Excel Formulas & Functions lesson. It develops the learner’s ability to apply this analytical method correctly, verify the result, and explain what it means.

formula

An expression beginning with = that calculates a spreadsheet result.

function

A named spreadsheet operation such as SUM, IF, or XLOOKUP.

range

A group of cells referred to together, such as B2:B10.

🧮 Practice Exercises
Understand the method, work through the data, verify the result, and explain the decision it supports.

Practice Exercises

Definition

Practice Exercises is a practical part of Excel Formulas & Functions: writing formulas and functions that transform spreadsheet values into repeatable results. The skill is complete only when the result is correct, reproducible, and understandable to its intended audience.

Detailed explanation

A formula should produce the same correct result whenever its source data changes and should be easy for another analyst to inspect. For this topic, begin with the business or research question, identify the required fields and units, then choose the simplest method that answers the question accurately.

Do not accept a result because the software produced it. Check source quality, formulas, filters, relationships, and comparison periods. The analyst—not the tool—remains responsible for the meaning of the result.

Step-by-step analytical workflow

  1. Define the analytical question, audience, period, units, and success measure.
  2. Inspect and clean the source before calculating or visualising anything.
  3. Apply Practice Exercises with the appropriate spreadsheet, Power BI, or SQL method.
  4. Cross-check totals, filters, data types, missing values, and assumptions.
  5. Explain the finding, limitation, and recommended decision in plain language.

Worked data example

RegionTargetActualVariance
Montserrado100118+18
Bong9081−9
Nimba110126+16

Method or formula:

=SUM(B2:B5)  |  =AVERAGE(B2:B5)  |  =IF(B2>=70,"Pass","Review")

Interpretation: In this sample, Montserrado and Nimba exceeded their targets while Bong was below target. A useful analyst would investigate why, check whether the comparison periods and units are consistent, and then recommend a specific action rather than reporting the numbers alone.

A
B
C
D

How to read this chart: Compare the bar heights to find the largest and smallest categories. A line chart would be more suitable if A–D represented consecutive time periods and the main question concerned change over time.

Professional best practices

  • Use relative and absolute references deliberately.
  • Handle missing or unexpected values explicitly.
  • Use Formula Auditing to trace important results.

Common mistakes and professional corrections

Common mistakeCorrection
Starting with a chart before defining the questionWrite the decision question and audience first.
Using unclean or inconsistently formatted dataProfile, clean, document, and validate the source.
Reporting a number without contextCompare it with a target, prior period, benchmark, or relevant segment.
📊 Practical task: Apply Practice Exercises to a small dataset from a school, shop, NGO, clinic, or public source. Save the working file, show the calculation or transformation, create one appropriate visual, and write a two-sentence insight and recommendation.

Chart-selection guide

  • Comparison: use a bar or column chart.
  • Trend over time: use a line chart.
  • Distribution: use a histogram or box plot.
  • Relationship: use a scatter plot.
  • Composition: use a stacked bar; use a pie only for a few simple parts of one whole.

Summary

Practice Exercises belongs to Excel Formulas & Functions. A capable analyst can explain the method, apply it to clean data, audit the result, select a truthful visual, and communicate the insight and recommended action.

Study tip: Keep the raw source unchanged. Work in a copy, label every transformation, and independently check one total before trusting the dashboard.

questions.question: Good analysis always ends with:
options: Clear insights and recommendations for decision-makers
questions.explanation: Insight and recommendations make analysis useful.

questions.question: Structured data is:
questions.explanation: Structured data fits neatly into tables.

questions.question: A KPI is a:
options: Key metric that measures performance against a goal
questions.explanation: KPIs track progress toward objectives.

questions.question: Data quality matters because:
options: Poor data leads to wrong conclusions
questions.explanation: Garbage in, garbage out — quality drives good analysis.

questions.question: A database differs from a spreadsheet in that it:
options: Handles large, related data more robustly
questions.explanation: Databases scale and enforce structure better than spreadsheets.

questions.question: Data ethics includes:
options: Respecting privacy and using data responsibly
questions.explanation: Handle data lawfully, fairly and with respect for privacy.

questions.question: Unstructured data includes:
questions.explanation: Unstructured data has no fixed tabular format.

questions.question: In Excel, a cell reference like B3 means:
questions.explanation: Columns are letters, rows are numbers: B3 = column B, row 3.

questions.question: Conditional formatting is used to:
questions.explanation: It formats cells that meet conditions (e.g. highlight top values).

questions.question: Sorting data lets you:
options: Arrange rows by a column’s values
questions.explanation: Sorting orders data ascending/descending.

lessons.title: 🧪 Portfolio Review
lessons.html:
Data Analysis · Module 20Excel · Power BI · Google Sheets

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Portfolio Review

Portfolio Review is the focus of this Assessments & Graduation lesson. It develops the learner’s ability to apply this analytical method correctly, verify the result, and explain what it means.

competency

The demonstrated ability to apply knowledge and skills to a required standard.

rubric

A scoring guide describing criteria and performance levels.

certificate

A credential confirming that stated completion requirements were met.

🎓 Portfolio Review
Understand the method, work through the data, verify the result, and explain the decision it supports.

Portfolio Review

Definition

Portfolio Review is a practical part of Assessments & Graduation: verifying completion, portfolio evidence, and demonstrated data-analysis competency. The skill is complete only when the result is correct, reproducible, and understandable to its intended audience.

Detailed explanation

A meaningful certificate represents successful assessments and project evidence that another person can review. For this topic, begin with the business or research question, identify the required fields and units, then choose the simplest method that answers the question accurately.

Do not accept a result because the software produced it. Check source quality, formulas, filters, relationships, and comparison periods. The analyst—not the tool—remains responsible for the meaning of the result.

Step-by-step analytical workflow

  1. Define the analytical question, audience, period, units, and success measure.
  2. Inspect and clean the source before calculating or visualising anything.
  3. Apply Portfolio Review with the appropriate spreadsheet, Power BI, or SQL method.
  4. Cross-check totals, filters, data types, missing values, and assumptions.
  5. Explain the finding, limitation, and recommended decision in plain language.

Worked data example

RegionTargetActualVariance
Montserrado100118+18
Bong9081−9
Nimba110126+16

Method or formula:

Lessons + Assessments + Projects + Capstone = Completion

Interpretation: In this sample, Montserrado and Nimba exceeded their targets while Bong was below target. A useful analyst would investigate why, check whether the comparison periods and units are consistent, and then recommend a specific action rather than reporting the numbers alone.

A
B
C
D

How to read this chart: Compare the bar heights to find the largest and smallest categories. A line chart would be more suitable if A–D represented consecutive time periods and the main question concerned change over time.

Professional best practices

  • Check missing requirements early.
  • Keep working links and accessible files.
  • Use the official learner name on the certificate.

Common mistakes and professional corrections

Common mistakeCorrection
Starting with a chart before defining the questionWrite the decision question and audience first.
Using unclean or inconsistently formatted dataProfile, clean, document, and validate the source.
Reporting a number without contextCompare it with a target, prior period, benchmark, or relevant segment.
📊 Practical task: Apply Portfolio Review to a small dataset from a school, shop, NGO, clinic, or public source. Save the working file, show the calculation or transformation, create one appropriate visual, and write a two-sentence insight and recommendation.

Chart-selection guide

  • Comparison: use a bar or column chart.
  • Trend over time: use a line chart.
  • Distribution: use a histogram or box plot.
  • Relationship: use a scatter plot.
  • Composition: use a stacked bar; use a pie only for a few simple parts of one whole.

Summary

Portfolio Review belongs to Assessments & Graduation. A capable analyst can explain the method, apply it to clean data, audit the result, select a truthful visual, and communicate the insight and recommended action.

Study tip: Keep the raw source unchanged. Work in a copy, label every transformation, and independently check one total before trusting the dashboard.
